features.description: Second-person plural pronoun or address form.
features.safe_example: Y'all can see why the answer matters.
features.blocked_context: Do not insert when no second-person reference exists.
features.source_reference: Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Second-person plural form.
features.safe_example: You'uns can see why she tried again.
features.blocked_context: Do not insert when no second-person reference exists.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Lexical item meaning afraid.
features.safe_example: He was afeared he would fail.
features.blocked_context: Use only when fear is already present in the anchor.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Regional lexical item for bag.
features.safe_example: She put it in a poke.
features.blocked_context: Use only where the anchor already mentions a bag.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Intensifier in phrases such as right hard or right much.
features.blocked_context: Use sparingly; do not create exaggerated rural voice.
features.source_reference: Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Negative quantifier meaning not any/no.
features.safe_example: He had nary a reason to quit.
features.blocked_context: Use only when the anchor already expresses absence or negation.
features.source_reference: Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Regional term referring to a small valley.
features.blocked_context: Do not add setting details absent from the anchor.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: A-prefix before certain -ing verb forms.
features.safe_example: He kept a-running down the road.
features.blocked_context: Use only with compatible -ing verbs; avoid excessive use.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Williams, 1992

features.description: Marks completed action or resultant state.
features.blocked_context: Use only when completion is already expressed.
features.source_reference: Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Stacked modal construction such as might could.
features.safe_example: He might could explain it better.
features.blocked_context: Do not add uncertainty or ability if the anchor does not contain it.
features.source_reference: Williams, 1992; Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Coreferential pronoun after a verb, often highlighting subject involvement.
features.safe_example: She wrote her a better answer.
features.blocked_context: Use only when a subject acts for their own benefit and meaning is preserved.
features.source_reference: Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Use of them before plural nouns.
features.blocked_context: Use only with plural noun phrases already present or naturally available.
features.source_reference: Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Modal-like construction listed in Appendix A.
features.safe_example: She used to could pass that test.
features.blocked_context: Do not add ability or past habitual meaning absent from the anchor.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Williams, 1992

features.description: Form listed as generic object in Appendix A.
features.blocked_context: Requires linguistic review before generation.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Reduced written form of them.
features.blocked_context: Use only where them already appears or is clearly implied.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Present-tense narration for past events.
features.safe_example: He comes in and says he will try again.
features.blocked_context: Do not shift time reference if it changes meaning.
features.source_reference: DART Appendix A; Labov, Ash, and Boberg, 2006

features.description: Near-miss marker meaning almost/nearly did.
features.blocked_context: Use only for near-miss or almost-event meanings already present.
features.source_reference: Yale Grammatical Diversity Project; Wolfram and Christian, 1976; Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Need + past participle construction without to be.
features.blocked_context: Use only where a needs-to-be/needs-ing passive meaning already exists.
features.source_reference: Yale Grammatical Diversity Project; Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Anymore used in non-negative contexts meaning nowadays/these days.
features.safe_example: People use computers for school anymore.
features.blocked_context: Use only where the time/aspect meaning is already compatible.
features.source_reference: Yale Grammatical Diversity Project; Wolfram and Schilling, 2016

features.description: Plumb used as an intensifier meaning completely/very.
features.blocked_context: Use sparingly and only where intensity is already present.
features.source_reference: Dictionary of American Regional English (DARE); Wolfram and Christian, 1976

safety_notes: Do not signal social class or intelligence through the rewrite.
Use grammatical features sparingly and only when they preserve the same proposition.
